title: An Underwater Shadow War Is Raging
gist: A review of Elisabeth Braw's Undersea War argues that cable and pipeline sabotage by Russia's shadow fleet and others is an under-appreciated shadow war against infrastructure carrying 95-99 percent of global internet traffic, where legal gaps and attribution problems favor attackers.

insights.claim: Between 95 and 99 percent of global internet traffic is carried by undersea cables, so damage to them has large consequences for communication, energy and most aspects of modern life.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Physical seabed infrastructure is a concentrated single point of failure for digital and energy systems; watch cable-cut incidents and repair timelines.
insights.locator: The author travels from the Red Sea to the Pacific

insights.claim: Public awareness of undersea cable vulnerability is low even though the cables are what actually run 'the cloud', which sits underwater rather than in the sky.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Low awareness means under-investment in redundancy and protection; hardening and repair-capacity providers are a possible beneficiary theme.
insights.quote: We assume ‘the cloud’ is in the sky, but it’s underwater
insights.locator: The seabed may be uninhabitable for humans

insights.claim: Cable routes are not orderly but 'squiggly' and precariously perched, described by one marine engineer as a spider's web, which makes them hard to protect.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Route complexity raises the number of exposed chokepoints.
insights.locator: The author travels from the Red Sea to the Pacific

insights.claim: In shallow waters submarines can glide right on top of pipelines and, even without hostile intent, can damage them, and tropical cyclones and undersea volcanoes have also severed cables.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Accidental or natural causes provide cover for deliberate attacks.
insights.locator: In shallow waters, submarines can glide

insights.claim: Russia is estimated to deploy a shadow fleet of at least 600 ships, many old requisitioned tankers flagged in places such as Guinea-Bissau, the Cook Islands, San Marino and Eswatini, used for sanctions-evading oil carriage and also for intelligence gathering, cable slashing and communications interference.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: The same fleet that circumvents oil sanctions doubles as a sabotage platform, linking energy sanctions enforcement to infrastructure risk.
insights.locator: Intelligence experts estimate that Russia is deploying a shadow fleet

insights.claim: Attackers benefit from ambiguity because motivation is hard to determine, crews on flag-of-convenience merchant vessels can claim an anchor accident, and many incidents happen in international waters beyond 12 nautical miles where coastal-state law does not apply.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Legal and attribution gaps lower the cost of sabotage, implying more incidents and slow retaliation.
insights.locator: It is sometimes hard to determine motivation

insights.claim: Defense experts say 'hybrid warfare' is now frowned upon as a term because it failed to galvanize publics, and 'shadow war' is preferred, covering disinformation, election interference and cyberattacks; even the August discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig airport, blamed on Russia by Berlin, has not made many European publics more alert.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Public complacency limits political appetite for defense and resilience spending in Europe.
insights.locator: I was at the Helsinki Security Forum

insights.claim: Cable cutting by Russian-linked vessels is the new element in a long history of Russian subsurface spying, starting with a November 2025 confrontation between the British military and the Russian vessel Yantar that then U.K. defense secretary John Healey made public.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Signals the shift of Russian activity from surveillance to disruption in Western European waters.
insights.locator: The Undersea War, by security analyst

insights.claim: Elisabeth Braw recounts incidents involving the Balticconnector, Nord Stream, C-Lion1, Arelion and Elisa cables, and says the threat is not limited to Russia.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Baltic energy and telecom links are the most repeatedly targeted assets.
insights.locator: Braw runs through a series of underwater or seafaring incidents

insights.claim: When a cable to Taiwan's Matsu Islands was snapped on Feb. 8, 2023, the 13,000 residents lost digital payments, shared information and most office work, and it took nearly two months for repairs to start and normality to return.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Shows how a single cable cut can function as coercion short of war against Taiwan's outlying islands.
insights.locator: The Matsu Islands is an archipelago

insights.claim: Great-power tensions are increasing at undersea pinch points including Taiwan, the high north and the Arctic, and the incident taught policymakers the importance of crisis management and early response without lessening the danger.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Monitor Arctic and Taiwan Strait cable and pipeline incidents as escalation indicators.
insights.locator: It took a while for the government in Taipei

insights.claim: The Trump administration, rather than strengthening international cooperation in this lawless arena, signed an executive order in April 2025 allowing deep-sea mining for rare-earth materials, including outside U.S. jurisdiction, in a bid to take on China, with no one knowing what damage the mining would cause.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Seabed mining could open a new rare-earth supply route and a new source of jurisdictional conflict; the resource estimates are described as only a 'hunch'.
insights.locator: The Trump administration, far from seeking

insights.claim: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the June 2025 NATO summit that the line between peace and war is now a 'fluid transition' rather than a digital zero or one, as Germany experiences daily attacks on data networks and submarine cables, and Braw concludes defenders have no manuals for this.
insights.speaker: John Kampfner
insights.so_what: Thresholds for Article 5-type responses to infrastructure sabotage remain undefined, raising the risk of miscalibrated escalation.
insights.quote: It’s no longer a digital zero or one, but rather a fluid transition
insights.locator: How far will any of the protagonists go?
